In [[algebraic geometry]], '''convexity''' is a restrictive technical condition for [[algebraic varieties]] originally introduced to analyze Kontsevich [[moduli space]]s <math>\overline{M}_{0,n}(X,\beta)</math> in [[quantum cohomology]].<ref name=":2">{{cite conference|last=Kontsevich|first=Maxim|authorlink=Maxim Kontsevich |contribution=Enumeration of Rational Curves Via Torus Actions|date=1995|title=The Moduli Space of Curves|series=Progress in Mathematics|volume=129|pages=335–368|editor-last=Dijkgraaf|editor-first=Robbert H.|editor-link=Robbert Dijkgraaf |publisher=Birkhäuser|location= Boston|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-4264-2_12|isbn=978-1-4612-8714-8|editor2-last=Faber|editor2-first=Carel F.|editor3-last=van der Geer|editor3-first=Gerard B. M.|arxiv=hep-th/9405035|s2cid=16131978}}</ref>{{rp|§1}}<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.ihes.fr/~maxim/TEXTS/WithManinCohFT.pdf|title=Gromov-Witten Classes, Quantum Cohomology, and Enumerative Geometry|last1=Kontsevich|first1=Maxim|last2=Manin|first2=Yuri|authorlink1=Maxim Kontsevich |authorlink2=Yuri Manin |date=|website=|page=9|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091128014639/http://www.ihes.fr:80/~maxim/TEXTS/WithManinCohFT.pdf |archive-date=2009-11-28 |access-date=}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite arXiv|last1=Fulton|first1=W.|last2=Pandharipande|first2=R.|date=1997-05-17|title=Notes on stable maps and quantum cohomology|eprint=alg-geom/9608011|pages=6,12,29,31}}</ref> These moduli spaces are smooth [[orbifold]]s whenever the target space is convex. A variety <math>X</math> is called convex if the pullback of the [[tangent bundle]] to a stable [[Algebraic curve|rational curve]] <math>f:C \to X</math> has globally generated sections.<ref name=":1" /> Geometrically this implies the curve is free to move around <math>X</math> infinitesimally without any obstruction. Convexity is generally phrased as the technical condition

: <math>H^1(C, f^*T_X) = 0</math>

since [[Serre's vanishing theorem]] guarantees this sheaf has globally generated sections. Intuitively this means that on a neighborhood of a point, with a vector field in that neighborhood, the local [[parallel transport]] can be extended globally. This generalizes the idea of [[convex set|convexity]] in [[Euclidean geometry]], where given two points <math>p,q</math> in a convex set <math>C \subset \mathbb{R}^n</math>, all of the points <math>tp + (1-t)q</math> are contained in that set. There is a vector field <math>\mathcal{X}_{U_p}</math> in a neighborhood <math>U_p</math> of <math>p</math> transporting <math>p</math> to each point <math>p' \in \{ tp + (1-t)q : t \in [0,1] \} \cap U_p</math>. Since the vector bundle of <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> is trivial, hence globally generated, there is a vector field <math>\mathcal{X}</math> on <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> such that the equality <math>\mathcal{X}|_{U_p} = \mathcal{X}_{U_{p}}</math> holds on restriction.

== Examples ==
There are many examples of convex spaces, including the following.

=== Spaces with trivial rational curves ===
If the only maps from a rational curve to <math>X</math> are constants maps, then the pullback of the tangent sheaf is the free sheaf <math>\mathcal{O}_C^{\oplus n}</math> where <math>n = \dim(X)</math>. These sheaves have trivial non-zero cohomology, and hence they are always convex. In particular, [[Abelian variety|Abelian varieties]] have this property since the [[Albanese variety]] of a rational curve <math>C</math> is trivial, and every map from a variety to an Abelian variety factors through the Albanese.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://mathoverflow.net/q/9066 |title=ag.algebraic geometry - Is there any rational curve on an Abelian variety?|website=MathOverflow|access-date=2020-02-28}}</ref>

=== Projective spaces ===
Projective spaces are examples of homogeneous spaces, but their convexity can also be proved using a [[sheaf cohomology]] computation. Recall the [[Euler sequence]] relates the tangent space through a short exact sequence

: <math>0 \to \mathcal{O} \to \mathcal{O}(1)^{\oplus (n+1)} \to \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{P}^n} \to 0</math>

If we only need to consider degree <math>d</math> embeddings, there is a short exact sequence

: <math>0 \to \mathcal{O}_C \to \mathcal{O}_C(d)^{\oplus (n+1)} \to f^*\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{P}^n} \to 0</math>

giving the long exact sequence

:<math>\begin{align}
0 & \to H^0(C,\mathcal{O}) \to  H^0(C,\mathcal{O}(d)^{\oplus(n+1)}) \to H^0(C,f^*\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{P}^n}) \\
& \to  H^1(C,\mathcal{O}) \to  H^1(C,\mathcal{O}(d)^{\oplus(n+1)}) \to  H^1(C,f^*\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{P}^n}) \to  0
\end{align}</math>

since the first two <math>H^1</math>-terms are zero, which follows from <math>C</math> being of genus <math>0</math>, and the second calculation follows from the [[Riemann–Roch theorem]], we have convexity of <math>\mathbb{P}^n</math>. Then, any nodal map can be reduced to this case by considering one of the components <math>C_i</math> of <math>C</math>.

=== Homogeneous spaces ===
Another large class of examples are homogenous spaces <math>G/P</math> where <math>P</math> is a parabolic subgroup of <math>G</math>. These have globally generated sections since <math>G</math> acts transitively on <math>X</math>, meaning it can take a bases in <math>T_xX</math> to a basis in any other point <math>T_yX</math>, hence it has globally generated sections.<ref name=":0" /> Then, the pullback is always globally generated. This class of examples includes [[Grassmannian]]s, projective spaces, and [[flag varieties]].

=== Product spaces ===
Also, products of convex spaces are still convex. This follows from the [[Coherent sheaf cohomology|Künneth theorem]] in coherent sheaf cohomology.

=== Projective bundles over curves ===
One more non-trivial class of examples of convex varieties are projective bundles <math>\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E})</math> for an algebraic vector bundle <math>\mathcal{E} \to C</math> over a smooth algebraic curve<ref name=":0" /><sup>pg 6</sup>.

== Applications ==
There are many useful technical advantages of considering moduli spaces of stable curves mapping to convex spaces. That is, the [[Kontsevich moduli space]]s <math>\overline{M}_{0,n}(X,\beta)</math> have nice geometric and deformation-theoretic properties.

=== Deformation theory ===
The deformations of <math>f:C \to X</math> in the [[Hilbert scheme]] of graphs <math>\operatorname{Hom}(C,X) \subset \operatorname{Hilb}_{C\times X/\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{C})}</math> has tangent space

: <math>T_{\operatorname{Hom}(C,X)}([f]) \cong H^0(C, f^*T_X)</math>&nbsp;&nbsp;<ref name=":2" />

where <math>[f] \in \operatorname{Hom}(C,X)</math> is the point in the scheme representing the map. Convexity of <math>X</math> gives the dimension formula below. In addition, convexity implies all infinitesimal deformations are unobstructed.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www-fourier.ujf-grenoble.fr/sites/ifmaquette.ujf-grenoble.fr/files/ete2011-maulik.pdf|title=Lectures on Donaldson-Thomas Theory|last=Maulik|first=Davesh|date=|website=|page=2|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200301003013/https://www-fourier.ujf-grenoble.fr/sites/ifmaquette.ujf-grenoble.fr/files/ete2011-maulik.pdf |archive-date=2020-03-01 |access-date=}}</ref>

=== Structure ===
These spaces are normal projective varieties of pure dimension

: <math>\dim(\overline{M}_{0,n}(X,\beta)) = \dim(X) + \int_\beta c_1(T_X) + n - 3</math>&nbsp;&nbsp;<ref name=":0" />

which are locally the quotient of a smooth variety by a finite group. Also, the open subvariety <math>\overline{M}_{0,n}^*(X,\beta)</math> parameterizing non-singular maps is a smooth fine moduli space. In particular, this implies the stacks <math>\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}(X,\beta)</math> are [[orbifold]]s.

=== Boundary divisors ===
The moduli spaces <math>\overline{M}_{0,n}(X,\beta)</math> have nice boundary divisors for convex varieties <math>X</math> given by

: <math>D(A,B;\beta_1,\beta_2) = \overline{M}_{0,A\cup \{\bullet \}}(X,\beta_1) \times_X \overline{M}_{0,B\cup \{\bullet \}}(X,\beta_2) </math>&nbsp;&nbsp;<ref name=":0" />

for a partition <math>A\cup B</math> of <math>[n]</math> and <math>\{ \bullet \}</math> the point lying along the [[Intersection theory|intersection]] of two rational curves <math>C = C_1 \cup C_2</math>.
